topStories.headline: SFSU Launches Campus-Wide Initiative to Connect Every Graduate With a Career
topStories.dek: President Mahoney announced the Future-Ready Workforce Initiative on Wednesday, the same day the university hosted its annual Fall Career & Internship Fair.
topStories.body:
San Francisco State University unveiled a new campus-wide workforce program on Wednesday, October 15, timed to coincide with its annual Fall Career & Internship Fair. The Future-Ready Workforce Initiative is designed to ensure every SFSU graduate leaves campus ready to compete in a rapidly shifting job market, according to a university press release.

The initiative pulls together faculty, students, alumni, administration, and a newly created senior position — assistant vice president for workforce partnerships — to build stronger ties between the university and Bay Area employers. Inés C. Barbosa joined SFSU this fall to fill that role, charged with expanding internship pipelines and employer relationships across the region.

An early concrete result is a paid internship program built through SFSU's partnership with San Francisco Federal Credit Union. Students placed through the program work alongside professionals in technology, marketing, human resources, and other departments, gaining experience and contacts before they graduate. The credit union's president and CEO, Ray Shams, said the program reflects both organizations' commitment to expanding educational opportunity and strengthening the regional workforce.

The announcement comes on the heels of SFSU's first year-over-year enrollment increase in more than a decade. Incoming fall 2026 student enrollment is up more than 18 percent compared to the prior year, giving the initiative an expanded pool of students to serve. Mayor Daniel Lurie issued a statement of support, saying the program connects students to the growing opportunities in San Francisco.

topStories.headline: Overnight Campers, 200-Plus at the Door: Raising Cane's Opens at Stonestown
topStories.dek: The chicken chain's second San Francisco location opened Monday at the former McDonald's space at 255 Winston Drive, drawing a crowd that began lining up the evening before.
topStories.body:
Last week this paper reported that Raising Cane's was set to open its second San Francisco location at Stonestown Galleria on Monday, October 13. It did — and the opening drew more than 200 people, with a handful of fans camping outside the mall overnight to be first in line, some arriving as early as 5:30 p.m. on Sunday, according to the San Francisco Chronicle.

The new location occupies 255 Winston Drive, the space previously held by a McDonald's that closed in 2024. On opening day, the first 20 customers received free meals for a year; others received merchandise including trucker hats. The grand opening also included a donation to Lowell High School's cheer team and a planned gift to the Children's Book Project, a nonprofit that provides books to underserved children, according to SFist.

Stonestown has become a notable outlier among San Francisco shopping centers. Its owner, Brookfield Properties, reported last year that the mall had nearly no vacancies, and the center extended its Friday and Saturday hours earlier this year. The contrast with the shuttered San Francisco Centre downtown — still searching for a new buyer after closing earlier in 2026 — has drawn wide notice from retail observers. The mall's location near SFSU, along with its parking and public transit access, has helped draw customers, according to retail experts quoted by the Chronicle.

topStories.headline: SFSU's Enrollment Rebound Is Real — But the Hole Left by a Decade of Decline Is Deep
topStories.dek: An SF Chronicle analysis published October 11 puts this fall's growth in context: SFSU shed nearly a quarter of its students between 2019 and 2024, taking faculty and revenue with them.
topStories.body:
Last week this paper reported that SFSU recorded its first enrollment increase in more than a decade. An SF Chronicle analysis published Sunday, October 11, fills in the difficult backstory and asks what the turnaround will actually require.

SFSU's student body shrank 22.3 percent between fall 2019 and fall 2024, dropping from roughly 29,000 students to about 22,600, according to federal data cited in the piece. Since 2024, the California State University chancellor's office has docked funding from campuses that missed enrollment targets — a policy that compounded the financial pressure on the campus. Among the side effects during the lean years: 45 percent of instructors and 12 percent of tenured professors departed.

President Lynn Mahoney, who announced in September that she will retire in summer 2027 after eight years leading the university, said SFSU is beginning this academic year with what she described as a healthy state budget after years of shortfalls, and touted new student enrollment up more than 10 percent for fall 2026. The CSU Board of Trustees is now conducting a national search for her successor; an advisory committee will include two faculty members elected by SFSU faculty, according to the October 5 CampusMemo.

For the neighborhoods surrounding SFSU's 19th Avenue campus — including Parkmerced, Lakeshore, and the Stonestown corridor — enrollment levels shape everything from foot traffic on Winston Drive to rental demand in nearby apartment buildings. A sustained rebound would be consequential well beyond the campus gates.

moreNews.headline: Empire Theater Site Could Become West Portal's Tallest Building Under Plans Filed in August
moreNews.body: Developer DM Development filed revised plans in late August 2026 to nearly triple the scope of a proposed housing project at 85 West Portal Avenue — the site of the long-vacant Empire Theater — expanding it from a nine-story, 64-unit building to a 12-story, 172-unit mixed-use complex. The expansion was made possible by the acquisition of an adjacent parcel at 59 West Portal Avenue and Mayor Daniel Lurie's 'Family Zoning' upzoning, combined with two state housing laws that allow the project to double its base residential density. The revised proposal includes 26 deed-restricted affordable units, 7,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, and parking for 89 cars. Handel Architects is the designer. The theater has been closed since Cinemark shut it during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. Local merchants said publicly they were concerned about disruption to West Portal Avenue's commercial strip. As of this week, no planning commission hearing date has been announced.
